messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi had always taken pride in his work as a plumber, navigating the tight spaces of Boston's old buildings with ease. But on one fateful night two years ago, everything changed. Kofi was working late on a job in Roxbury when he was assaulted by a group of teenagers who had been lurking around the site. They beat him severely, leaving him with broken ribs and a deep gash above his left eyebrow. As Kofi lay in the hospital recovering from his injuries, he couldn't shake off the feeling that he should have seen it coming. He replayed the events leading up to the attack over and over in his mind, wondering if there was something he could have done differently. These visual memories of the assault haunted him – the flash of a knife, the sound of footsteps behind him, the feel of fists pummeling his chest. Kofi's wife, Ama, tried her best to support him during this time, but Kofi felt like he was losing himself. He had always defined himself by his work and his ability to provide for his family; now, every creaking pipe or unexpected noise made him jump, sending his heart racing as if he were back in that abandoned lot. Even the thought of going to a new job site filled him with dread – what if something happened again? What if he wasn't prepared? As time went on, Kofi found himself retreating into a very small safe zone – his own home, specifically his favorite armchair by the window. It was the only place where he felt truly secure, surrounded by familiar sights and sounds. But even this sanctuary had its limits; every night, Kofi would lie awake for hours, listening to the city outside, waiting for... something. He couldn't quite put it into words – just a creeping sense of danger that seemed to seep in through the walls. Kofi tried to talk to Ama about his fears, but he found himself struggling to articulate them. The memories were there, etched vividly in his mind's eye, but whenever he tried to verbalize them, they slipped away like sand between his fingers. He felt guilty for not being able to put into words what had happened – as if somehow, it was all still his fault. At work, Kofi started avoiding new jobs or any situation that might put him in an unfamiliar environment. His clients began to notice the change; some even complained about his tardiness and lack of focus. But for Kofi, every creaking pipe or groaning floorboard was a potential threat – he couldn't shake off the feeling that he was walking on eggshells, just waiting for something to go wrong. Ama tried to reassure him, but Kofi couldn't help feeling like he'd lost his edge. He used to be capable of handling anything; now, every little thing made him doubt himself. What if he wasn't doing the right thing? What if... what if... what if... Two years after the assault, Kofi's listlessness and self-doubt had started to take a toll on their marriage. Ama encouraged him to seek help, but Kofi was hesitant – what would people think? Would they see him as weak? Finally, it was Ama who made the appointment for him with a therapist. As Kofi sat in the waiting room, clutching his wife's hand like a lifeline, he knew that something had to give. He couldn't keep living in this perpetual state of hypervigilance, always on edge and forever trapped in his own private nightmare. What scared Kofi most was losing himself completely – losing the sense of self-worth that had defined him for so long. As he looked at Ama, her eyes filled with worry and love, he knew he had to try.
